citation: 'To Ban or Not to Ban: Uses and Gratifications of Mobile Phones among Township High School Learners' (arXiv)
mechanisms: Physical safety and economic survival bind device carriage decisions more tightly than institutional bans: theft risk and data unaffordability make leaving the phone at home a rational protection strategy
Peer connection and privacy from authorities outweigh instructional attention because constant communication sustains social bonds that classroom supervision cannot replicate
Communication mode selection is cost-driven, as the primary evaluation metric ahead of pedagogical preference: high voice tariffs push substitution toward text and voice notes
Mobile phones function as essential infrastructure substituting for computers because lower maintenance costs make them the only viable digital tool for daily routines and schoolwork

Security concerns legitimize device possession independent of educational utility because emergency risks in township environments render connectivity a safety necessity rather than a recreational luxury
objection_patterns: Will I be robbed carrying this device to school?
Can I afford the data bundles required to use this?
Does this help me search for answers when I have no computer?
Will this keep me safe during emergencies?
confidence: Qualitative survey and interviews in township high schools; mechanisms reflect attested learner rationales, magnitudes and generalizability unknown. Note: this card was originally drafted alongside Goodman et al. (2011) as a second source, but that paper is quantitative/correlational and contributed no extractable passages — it is not a valid citation for this card and has been removed.
